import { Code } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'
import models from '../../../../snippets/models.ts?raw'

Familiar reaches models through Pi's `Models` registry. `createModels()` starts empty. You register each provider yourself and pass a credential store the providers read and refresh.

```ts
import { createModels } from '@familiar-ai/core/models'
import { openaiProvider } from '@familiar-ai/core/models/openai'
import { openrouterProvider } from '@familiar-ai/core/models/openrouter'

const models = createModels({ credentials })
models.setProvider(openaiProvider())
models.setProvider(openrouterProvider())
```

`credentials` is a `CredentialStore` your host owns. It must persist, or every restart signs out. The daemon's [file store](https://github.com/AidanZealley/familiar/blob/main/apps/daemon/src/credentials.ts) is a working Node example.

Keep provider credentials on the server. Never put them in frontend code.

## ChatGPT sign-in

ChatGPT sign-in lets a Familiar use a ChatGPT subscription instead of an API key. It's the model's access, not a login to your app. Pass `account`, and Familiar signs in through the same `models`:

<Code code={models} lang="ts" title="assistant.ts" />

The `./host.ts` imports stand in for your own code. `deviceId` returns a stable ID for this installation; OpenAI identifies the app's logins by it.

With `account`:

- `workspace.account` exposes `state()`, `signIn()`, `answer(text)`, `cancelSignIn()`, `signOut()` and `onChange(listener)`.
- The state is one of `signed-in`, `signed-out`, `expired` or `signing-in`. While signing in it carries the provider's `url` and `paste: true` when the provider needs the address the browser ended on.
- The HTTP API serves these under `/account` and streams the state, so a UI can run the whole sign-in.
- The workspace closes the account when it's dismissed. Every Familiar in it uses the one login.

Without an account, the host keeps credentials working itself and a failed request fails like any other.

## Model choices

`modelChoices` lists the models the installation offers, each with the reasoning level it starts on. `chatModel` is what a new Familiar's chat starts on, and people may switch a Familiar to any other choice. Leave `modelChoices` out and the only choice is `chatModel` at medium.

Memory's filing and consolidation run on `chatModel` unless you set `memoryModel`, which can be a cheaper model: background memory work needs less than a chat does. Each Familiar can pick its own from the choices too (`familiars.update(id, { memoryModel })`; `null` returns it to the workspace's), applying from its next memory call. Both must be in `modelChoices`, and are run at the level listed there.

Each Familiar remembers its current model and level. Change them with its `setModel(ref)` and `setThinkingLevel(level)`, from `workspace.familiars.get(id)`, or over HTTP under `/familiars/:familiar/model`. Both throw a `ModelError` for a choice that isn't on offer.
